entry.title: Do not buy RAM, compress
entry.content:
Do not buy RAM, compress!

AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram, a solution to compress memory.

Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled.

Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.

I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half!

How it looks in practice

I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics)

If we look at the running apps, then we see it should not fit.

In the memory usage we see that some demand was placed into the zram swap space.

In the terminal we can check how much memory is used, and we can calculate the compression ratio.

5.7G of data in 1.7G of RAM. That’s a compression ratio of 1:3.35.

Getting started

Compressing RAM is something which helps to get you more out of your own hardware, but also out of your cloud environment. Do more with less.

The Arch Linux wiki has a good article on how to get started.

entry.title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
entry.content:
It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output.

That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch.

We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end?

While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record.

NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash.

Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly.

The Short VersionPrices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking.SSDs should turn first. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027.Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories.2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing.Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first.Where Prices Stand in September 2026

Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records.

DriveSept 2025Sept 2026ChangeSeagate IronWolf 4TB (HDD)€94€195+108%WD Red Plus 8TB (HDD)€170€349+105%Toshiba MG09 18TB (HDD)€288€858+198%Seagate BarraCuda 24TB (HDD)€308€804+161%Kingston NV3 1TB (SSD)€50€144+189%Samsung 990 Pro 4TB (SSD)€285€609+114%

Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers.

The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this.

The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns.

Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times

Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways.

SSDs follow the chip market

SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too.

Hard drives follow multi-year contracts

Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall.

The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say

TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026.

At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter, with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND, and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay.

Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027.

New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down.

Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024.

You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history. That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027: DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises.

The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028

For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop.

Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead.

Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached.

Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices.

So where does hard drive relief come from?

Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction.

Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed.

A Realistic Timeline

Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once.

Rest of 2026 Still rising, but slowly Small monthly increases for both hard drives and SSDs. Black Friday may bring a handful of genuine deals on specific SSDs, but no broad drop. The NAND market stays in deficit.First half of 2027 The plateau SSD contract prices flatten as new flash supply builds. Hard drive prices hold at their peak under long-term contracts. DRAM remains very tight, so Macs and PCs stay expensive.Second half of 2027 SSDs start to ease NAND supply and demand move into balance. Portable and internal SSD prices begin a gradual decline, with the largest capacities, which rose most, likely to fall most. Hard drives stay broadly flat.2028 onwards Hard drives follow As current contracts roll off and HAMR drives dominate data centres, hard drive cost per terabyte should improve. Prices should settle meaningfully below today's levels, but probably above 2024's.What Could Change the Timeline

It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices.

It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers.

Signals worth watchingA flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way.ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard.New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite.Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving.Should You Buy Now or Wait?

That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it.

You need storage for paid work this yearBuy now

Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices.

Your backups are incompleteBuy now

A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how.

You want a fast SSD upgrade that can waitWait if you can

SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall.

You are stockpiling "just in case"Don't

Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased.

Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have

The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged.

See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one.Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison, and reclaim the space safely.Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive.Search files on unplugged drives, so shelved archives stay useful. Here is how offline search works.Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues.

If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices.

Frequently Asked QuestionsWhen will hard drive prices come down?

Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut.

When will SSD prices come down?

TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop.

Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels?

Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast.

Should I buy a hard drive now or wait?

If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect.

Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026?

AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking.

The Bottom Line

Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts.

The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change.

entry.title: What's New in PHP 8.6
entry.content:
PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language, with new features including Partial Function Application, a new Duration class, a Polling API, and a new clamp() function

More expressive code, stronger types, and scalable I/O.

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest.

\Time\Duration Class

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch.

Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP.

clamp() Function

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range.

SortDirection Enum

A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries.

Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor.

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it.

$versions = ['8.4', '8.5', '8.6', '8.7', '9.0']; $supportsPfa = array_filter( $versions, fn ($version) => version_compare($version, '8.6', '>='), );

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way.

/** * All delays are in microseconds. */ function backoff( int $baseDelay, int $step, int $attempt, ): void { $delay = $baseDelay + ($step * (2 ** $attempt)); // Wait at most 30 seconds. usleep(min($delay, 30_000_000)); } // 1 second base delay, plus 100 milliseconds // doubling with each attempt. backoff(1_000_000, 100_000, $attempt);use Time\Duration; function backoff( Duration $baseDelay, Duration $step, int $attempt, ): void { $delay = $baseDelay->add($step->multiplyBy(2 ** $attempt)); // Durations are comparable, so min() works directly. $delay = min($delay, Duration::fromSeconds(30)); time_nanosleep($delay->seconds, $delay->nanoseconds); } backoff( Duration::fromSeconds(1), Duration::fromMilliseconds(100), $attempt, ); // Preconfigure the delays using Partial Function Application. $waitBeforeRetry = backoff( Duration::fromSeconds(1), Duration::fromMilliseconds(100), attempt: ?, ); $waitBeforeRetry($attempt);

The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select(). It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on.

$server = stream_socket_server('tcp://0.0.0.0:8080'); $clients = []; while (true) { $read = [$server, ...$clients]; $write = $except = null; // Based on select(), which typically can't handle // more than 1024 connections stream_select($read, $write, $except, null); foreach ($read as $stream) { if ($stream === $server) { $clients[] = stream_socket_accept($server); continue; } $data = fread($stream, 8192); if ($data === '' || $data === false) { $key = array_search($stream, $clients, true); unset($clients[$key]); fclose($stream); } else { fwrite($stream, $data); } } }use Io\Poll\{Context, Event}; $server = stream_socket_server('tcp://0.0.0.0:8080'); // Automatically uses epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll $poll = new Context(); $poll->add(new StreamPollHandle($server), [Event::Read]); while (true) { foreach ($poll->wait() as $watcher) { $stream = $watcher->getHandle()->getStream(); if ($stream === $server) { $client = stream_socket_accept($server); $poll->add( new StreamPollHandle($client), [Event::Read], ); continue; } $data = fread($stream, 8192); if ($data === '' || $data === false) { $watcher->remove(); fclose($stream); } else { fwrite($stream, $data); } } }

Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler.

$config = @file_get_contents('/etc/app/config.json'); if ($config === false) { // Only an unstructured message string is available $error = error_get_last(); log_error($error['message']); }$context = stream_context_create([ 'stream' => [ 'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode::Exception, ], ]); try { $config = file_get_contents( '/etc/app/config.json', context: $context, ); } catch (StreamException $e) { foreach ($e->getErrors() as $error) { // $error->code is a StreamErrorCode enum case log_error( $error->code->name, $error->message, $error->wrapperName, ); } }

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned.

var_dump(max(0, min(-10, 100))); // int(0) var_dump(max(0, min(50, 100))); // int(50) var_dump(max(0, min(110, 100))); // int(100)var_dump(clamp(-10, 0, 100)); // int(0) var_dump(clamp(50, 0, 100)); // int(50) var_dump(clamp(110, 0, 100)); // int(100) // Any comparable value works with clamp(). This // includes the new Duration class. var_dump(clamp( \Time\Duration::fromSeconds(30), min: \Time\Duration::fromMinutes(1), max: \Time\Duration::fromMinutes(10), )->seconds); // int(60)

The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code.

Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog.

class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy( string $column, int $direction = SORT_ASC, ): static { $this->orderBy[] = $column . ' ' . match ($direction) { SORT_ASC => 'ASC', SORT_DESC => 'DESC', }; return $this; } } $qb->orderBy('name', SORT_DESC); $qb->orderBy('name', SORT_STRING); // Accepted by the signature, then fails inside the method: // UnhandledMatchError: Unhandled match case 2class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy( string $column, SortDirection $direction = SortDirection::Ascending, ): static { $this->orderBy[] = $column . ' ' . match ($direction) { SortDirection::Ascending => 'ASC', SortDirection::Descending => 'DESC', }; return $this; } } $qb->orderBy('name', SortDirection::Descending); $qb->orderBy('name', SORT_STRING); // TypeError: QueryBuilder::orderBy(): Argument #2 ($direction) // must be of type SortDirection, int given

Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag.

class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. * * @param string $query Terms to search * @param int $limit Maximum number of results */ public function search(string $query, int $limit = 10): array { return []; } } // Parameter descriptions can only be extracted // by parsing the function's DocComment.class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. */ public function search( /** Terms to search */ string $query, /** Maximum number of results */ int $limit = 10, ): array { return []; } } var_dump( new ReflectionParameter([DB::class, 'search'], 'query') ->getDocComment(), ); // string(22) "/** Terms to search */"ReflectionProperty::isReadable() and ReflectionProperty::isWritable() Methods

With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods.

class NewsEntry { public string $title = 'PHP 8.6 released!'; public private(set) string $slug = 'php-86-released'; } $entry = new NewsEntry(); foreach (['title', 'slug'] as $item) { $property = new ReflectionProperty(NewsEntry::class, $item); printf( "%s: isReadable=%s isWritable=%s\n", $item, $property->isReadable(null, $entry) ? 'yes' : 'no', $property->isWritable(null, $entry) ? 'yes' : 'no', ); } // title: isReadable=yes isWritable=yes // slug: isReadable=yes isWritable=no

Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it.

interface Rule { public string $parser { get; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser; public function __construct() { $this->parser = SlugParser::class; } }#[\Override] attribute can now be applied to class constants and enum cases.__debugInfo() magic method.Config::DEFAULTS->timeout = 30.Uri\Rfc3986\UriBuilder and Uri\WhatWg\UrlBuilder classes build URIs from their components, along with new methods for detecting URI and host types and a Uri\WhatWg\url_percent_encode() function.mysqli::quote_string() method escapes a string and wraps it in quotes, matching PDO::quote().pack() and unpack() now accept the < and > endianness modifiers on integer and float format codes.error_include_args INI setting consistently includes function arguments in error messages.grapheme_strrev() function reverses strings by grapheme cluster, and the new IntlNumberRangeFormatter class formats ranges of numbers.ZipArchive::openString() and ZipArchive::closeString() methods work with in-memory archives.array_map() with first-class callable or partial application callbacks into loops, faster printf() calls, caching of stateless closures, and faster JSON encoding.return inside a finally block is now deprecated, as it silently discards exceptions and overrides values returned from the try or catch block.__construct() or __destruct() is now deprecated, as is making them generators. Declaring a nullable return type for let or is as the name of a class, function, or constant is now deprecated. Using _ as a constant name, namespace as a class constant name, or readonly as a function name is also deprecated.mb_ereg() and mb_split() have been deprecated, as the underlying Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PCRE functions with the u modifier can be used instead.is_double(), is_long(), is_integer(), and doubleval() aliases have been deprecated. Use get_object_vars() to convert the object first.strcoll() and the SORT_LOCALE_STRING sort flag have been deprecated. entry.title: Unblockable communication with gravity
Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
entry.content:
Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app

A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work.

If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue.

I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes.

Why fanzines.app exists

The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down:

┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐ │ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°) ├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤ │ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app.

In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server.

Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine.

Fixing how pages are paired

In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover.

It looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left.

The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order.

I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it.

Smaller changes that make the editor less fussy

When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them.

I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs (X, Y, Width, Height). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection.

The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text.

Before downloading the PDF, a Review step shows the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact.

A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish. Changing the language keeps your current pages.

Thanks for reading, Wil

You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app

entry.title: OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
entry.content:
October 27, 2026 Â· kixelated

OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem

On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News.

thx

A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant. You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didnât.

Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over. deus vult

Hot Take Alert

Letâs say youâre a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product. Letâs say youâre making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash. Letâs say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France?

If your AI ever replies with:

Iâm sorry, you broke up, can you repeat that?

You fucked up. You picked WebRTC for voice AI.

The Danger that Lurks Beneath

You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPTâ¢. You click on the microphone and grunt:

What is le capital of France?

OH NO, hypothetical sudden packet loss. A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable. All too common Iâm afraid.

WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices. It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time. Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old.

This kind of sucks for a voice AI product. You walk out of wifi range, hit a cellular dead zone, or starlink terminal switches satellites. Oops, your tokens are wasted, or worse, AI tries to guess what you said.

WebRTC can usually detect packet loss and retransmit. But retransmissions are disabled by default for audio. And even when enabled, the audio jitter buffer wonât wait for them.

But why not? Isnât this networking 101? Just send that shit again?

Itâs because of us.

The Speed of You

We flesh bags consume/produce audio in âreal-timeâ, aka a human clock rate. Our neurons can only fire so fast.

For a real-time conferencing product like Google Meet, latency needs to be near zero. Any delay is super fucking annoying, which is why WebRTC does everything in its power to minimize it.

Blocking on retransmissions will cause delays. Itâs the fatal flaw with TCP and why WebRTC is UDP based in the first place. And worse yet, retransmissions will cause a rapid burst of audio on recovery.

This is a bad user experience. Humans do not want to wait, then process a burst of audio at 10x speed. WebRTC instead primarily* relies on human retransmissions.

You: What is le â¦ France?

Me:

You: I said, what is le capital of France?

* Before a WebRTC warrior flames me on LinkedIn, read the fix it fix it fix it section.

Are we doomed to mediocrity?

Clock That Solder Boy

Of course not. Wake up old man, itâs not 2020 any longer. The internet is no longer for our flabby lips.

Our robot overlords produce/consume audio based on a silicon clock rate. We shoved electricity into a rock and now it can read a library in minutes. What a time to be alive.

Voice agents can hear and speak audio faster than real-time. Listening at 20x the speed? No problem. Speaking at 20x the speed? No problem.

Humans stuck at real-time. We speak too slowly, so speech-to-text has to wait for us. We hear too slowly, so text-to-speech has to wait for us.

WebRTC is designed for humans, not voice AI agents. These poor robots are being held back by our mediocrity.

I Require Context

When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird.

Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can. However, LLMs are blocked on context.

Hereâs a dumb example of context growing over time:

1s: What 2s: What is 3s: What is le 4s: What is le capital 5s: What is le capital of 6s: What is le capital of France?

If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck. France is le gatekeeper, and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite. In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet.

Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken? WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty. The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU) noticing a thing.

So thatâs what Mr. MoQ does. No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio.

Itâs not expensive either: audio is tiny. 1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets. We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact.

And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time!

The model no longer has to guess. It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either. This is a pure user experience win.

Not Just Mics

Guess what? WebRTC doesnât just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS.

Fun Fact: WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives, not when it is supposed to be rendered. Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal. Sure, itâll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio.

This is a huge problem for voice AI. TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp. But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTCâ¦ the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet.

And if thereâs any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada.

If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet. A stamp of sorts.

Random Access Memory

Welcome back to the future Marty. We faster than real-time now.

RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive. And being able to store stuff locally. You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers.

We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM. Absurd, I know.

Itâs how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity. MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI. Your sick baking recipe wonât be subject to surprise congestion.

And donât you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB. Youâre not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick.

Disclaimer: this behavior is not IETF standardized. Itâs something only my moq.dev clients (and thus Pipecat) support. Be my guest if you want to argue with Cisco and get it into the official standards.

Enter the Antagonist

Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC?

WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio. Itâs available in every browser via libwebrtc, a C++ monolith maintained by Google. Itâs so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else.

The problem is that WebRTC is the Google Meet client. It is designed specifically for Googleâs conferencing product, not their voice AI product (they use WebSocket), and certainly not your product.

quite the anti-competitive ruse tbh. Google can ship product updates without consulting the other browser vendors. No other conferencing app can do this on the web.

Fun Fact: This is why every other conferencing app recommends a native client. Otherwise, they can only reach parity with Google Meet at best. Native apps can do whatever they want over UDP instead.

Fix It Fix It Fix It

So thatâs why your hyper deluxe ChatGPTâ¢ voice AI model, after billions invested, has the audacity to ask: can you repeat that?

I could dump on WebRTC for days, but I want to be positive for a change. Hereâs how to fix it.

First off, I need to acknowledge what WebRTC does have:

NetEQ is amazing. It changes audio playback speed based on jitter. But not packet loss. Audio retransmissions can now be enabled via SDP munging (disgusting). But the NetEQ jitter buffer wonât wait for them. The playout-delay RTP extension is perfect for voice AI. But itâs video only.

To fix WebRTC, we need to petition Google to:

Implement playout-delay for audio. Allow the jitter buffer to grow, both in the past and into the future (for TTS). Render audio based on timestamps not vibes. IDK some RTP extension to bump the track generation (for interruptions).

And of course, petition the wider WebRTC ecosystem to do the same.

Gatekept

The main problem with WebRTC will remain: Google is the gatekeeper.

Your Claude friend canât just fork libwebrtc and fix these issues. Google is required for web support, at least until Theo spends $420k to rewrite Chromium in Rust.

I think itâs amazing that playout-delay was merged 10 years ago and audio still doesnât have it. Higher latency/quality playback has never been a priority for WebRTC, since Google Meet is the only product that matters.

Fun Fact: This is why I ended up creating MoQ. We tried using WebRTC at Twitch but the real-time-or-else made for a poor user experience. I am but a humble software engineer, and despite trying, we failed to petition Google.

But OpenAI has enough sway to fix WebRTC. One long-deserved improvement is WARP (not that WARP), which was hot on the heels of my last blog post. Keep at it Justin, or join the Dark Side with me.

Enter The Protagonist

In my humble and handsome opinion, itâs time to invest in a better transport. Take a few of the Mâs from the Bâs and Tâs; nobody will notice.

A voice agent should never ask the user to retransmit a prompt. A voice agent should instead ask the transport to retransmit a prompt.

Spoiler alert: Media over QUIC is that better transport btw.

Pipecat now supports MoQ! A huge thank you to Vanessa and Claude Code for putting in the work and putting up with my constant âimprovementsâ.

Hereâs a crude demo with my credit card deets attached. please donât milk me dry.

Note that Iâve only spent like a day of work prompting on this. It took me significantly longer to write this damn blog post. Donât judge too harshly pls.

And yes, it sometimes says âcan you repeat that?â which is hilariously ironic. The first/last hop is MoQ, but I donât control the rest of the pipeline. If Deepgram, OpenAI, or Cartesia drop ur packets then thereâs nothing I can do about it.

Interruptions

Weâre not done yet. I wanted to shill the MoQ in the middle of the blog and use the restâ¦

Sometimes the AI is monologuing and you need to tell it to STFU. Itâs pretty easy to do with WebRTC because of the sleep before sending each packet. But with MoQ, we need some signal to tell the player to abandon the playout buffer.

Hereâs the naive approach without a signal:

notdo this on my first implementation.

My solution for this is deviously clever. So clever.

For MoQ, weâve prioritized the ability to add/remove tracks dynamically. Most media protocols have fixed tracks and itâs a pain in the butt: HLS, DASH, RTMP, WebRTC, etc. You canât add 1080p, or switch codecs, after a broadcast is live.

My super clever idea is to reuse this functionality for interruptions. Just make a new audio track (and remove the old one) as the STFU Signalâ¢.

This works on a generic MoQ player. We automatically switch tracks, using timestamps to keep synchronization.

ez

Butt-to-Butt

Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. You didnât mention speech-to-speech?

Look, Dunning-Kruger is the only reason the previous blog post exists. I didnât know speech-to-speech existed until the comment section. What can I say but ur welcome.

DISCLAIMER: I still havenât done any research on the state of voice AI. I give you full permission to tweet @kixelated ur stupid.

The idea behind speech-to-speech is to cut out the text middleman. The disjoint STT -> LLM -> TTS pipelines get smashed together, reducing latency while preserving verbal context. OpenAI is the pioneer in this space and they deserve mad props.

So this vindicates WebRTC right? The speech-to-speech latency can be low enough to justify dropping packets?

Not so fast literary strawman. Thereâs a fundamental trade-off between latency and quality.

Latency Budgets

The more time you have to work on something, the better the result. Good things take time, like Fable changing a single line in README.md because Iâm too poor to pay 3.5x for ultrafast.

Networks are the same. The more time you have to transmit something, the better the quality. Itâs why retransmits exist in the first place.

Unless youâre doing broadcast TV, which still uses MPEG-TS and still results in glitchy messes. Seriously wtf guys, TV is no longer over the air, and we donât need 188 byte packets any longer.

Anyway, the amount of time a user is willing to wait for something is a product decision. Put on your big boye pants, itâs time to be a PM. Do users want something fast and lossy, or slow and reliable?

Why not both?

Thatâs the idea behind speech-to-speech. Do a low-latency STS pass for easy prompts and to generate filler noise.

Human: What is le capital of France?

ChatGPT: One second, let me look that up.

Boom, even that useless âIâm thinkingâ response makes the human feel good chemicals. But more importantly for us anti-PMs, it buys us enough time to start a slower pass.

I donât work at a frontier lab so this is all speculation, but I imagine STT->LLM->TTS is still used for these slower passes. A STS model with Astra/Fable quality is absolutely idealâ¦ but probably not worth the investment.

Either way, doesnât matter if itâs STS or STT->LLM->TTS. The only thing that matters is the latency budget.

MoQ do Both

One of the core problems weâre trying to fix with MoQ is the whole âone transport per latencyâ issue in the industry. Itâs face-palmingly common to use different protocols based on the latency budget.

For example, an all-hands presentation where the speakers use Zoom, while everybody else watches via HLS and canât participate.

Fuck that noise, MoQ supports multiple latency targets with a single connection. In the case of voice AI:

real-time latency for rapid replies (STS). loss-less quality for slow replies (STT->LLM->TTS).

How? Every MoQ subscription includes how long the subscriber is willing to wait.

Your real-time model can have a maximum latency of 500ms while your more accurate model might have a maximum latency of 5s. Both get coalesced into a single upstream subscription which can fanout.

And note that this is the maximum latency. The latency is 0 except during terrible network conditions, and eventually we give up. This is the core difference between MoQ and TCP/WebSocket for Voice AI.

Your transport latency should be aligned with your product latency budget.

Itâs Simple: Predict the Future

One more strawman to beat into the dirt.

Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. WebRTC doesnât care about packet loss because it uses FEC.

M8 go read my previous blog posts: never use datagrams and forward error correction. This is like my dumber one hot take.

WebRTC (and Opus) include Forward Error Correction to help mask packet loss. The idea is to stuff a crappier, lower bitrate copy of the previous audio frame into the next packet.

But only a single last packet. It canât even handle two lost packets in a row, let alone a full network blip.

This is fine for WebRTC because it doesnât give a shit about audio older than 30ms. But itâs not fine for voice AI or really anything on the internet. Packet loss due to congestion is bursty, not random.

A common âfixâ is to spread these copies over time, so you can handle X lost packets in a row. See Opus 1.5. All of this extra data has a real cost, and if you donât know what youâre doing (and you donât), then you will aggravate bufferbloat.

In my humble (and attractive) opinion, FEC is best for huge RTTs, like transmitting to le moon. In <current year>, we instead use CDNs to shrink the lossy first/last mile which makes retransmissions OP. Why send more bytes spread over 400ms, instead of retransmitting in 40ms?

But if a WebRTC warrior insists, QUIC libraries can retransmit stream data as many times as they want. Basically RED but based on byte offsets, not packets, and fully transparent to the receiver. Thatâs a free idea btw.

More Free Ideas

I should end the blog post here but seriously, Iâm 3 weeks in and need this shit forwarded internally. Take a screenshot of it on your internal Slack.

Hey, OpenAI. Iâm sorry for flaming you for representing state-of-the-art for voice AI. We may have gotten off on the wrong foot.

Hey, Anthropic. Iâm sorry that I called you the orange butthole company. We may have gotten off on the wrong foot.

Iâll make it up to both of you. Hereâs some free ideas you could prototype with your unlimited Fable/Astro 7 tokens. Just give me Co-Authored-By credit on the git commits. Or Scion, I donât care.

Please I need more green squares on my Github.

You can spot the exact moment I started token maxxing.

Decouple Compute

I know you have obscene amounts of capital, but getting GPUs next to every single user in the world is hard. But getting cheap DELL servers next to every single user in the world is easy.

Run moq-relay within CDN edges. Run models where GPUs are available.

Like I said earlier, this is basically the premise of CDNs. A huge number of edge nodes close to users minimizes the congested first/last mile. Over-provision the backbone so you can get the traffic to the GPUs without congestion.

You can independently scale network and compute.

Which I hope you guys already do, and are big enough to justify a custom Voice AI protocol instead of using a standardized MoQ implementation.

For everybody else, MoQ is generic enough to serve more than just Voice AI. Think of MoQ like a live HTTP. Itâs an IETF standard after all, the same body that does that HTTP thing.

In fact, my first big customer is using moq.pro to mass fanout JSON blobs. Literally a generic pub/sub protocol masquerading as an A/V protocol.

Prioritize Context

Iâm a transport and ideas guy, not an AI scientist. Donât flame me if this is obvious and/or impossible.

The core problem with WebRTC+AI is that thereâs a disconnect between the model and the transport. This blog focused on aligning latencyâ¦ but what about aligning context?

After all, not all tokens have the same weight. If we knew the relative importance of each token, we could use that to make informed networking decisions.

high priority: what capital france low priority: is le zero priority: <silence>

To implement this via MoQ, you would split the audio track into separate tracks that are encoded independently. The high priority track would get first dibs on available bandwidth, and the subscriber would wait longer for it.

But TBH the hard part is actually giving a shit. Audio bitrates are so low that you rarely get a chance to prioritize anyway, and itâs not worth the hassle of doing a client-side tokenizer. Maybe it could matter for video tho.

Back-fill that Boye

The other problem with dropping audio after 30ms is that itâs a one-way door.

Bold prediction: The next Claudism will be one-way door after itâs been trained on this post.

Once a network transport decides to drop data over the network, it canât be used for other things. Now, I donât know if frontier labs store raw audioâ¦ but maybe they should.

Eventually the AI model has to stop waiting and guess based on incomplete data. Did it do a good job or bad job? How can we know?

Wellâ¦ maybe donât actually drop the audio; keep that shit in RAM. Audio is tiny after all. We can set max-latency to 10 minutes and it will be transmitted eventually at the lowest priority. We backfill that boye only when the network has fully recovered.

Why backfill via MoQ? Why not save it as a file and train on it later?

Vroom vroom, the GPU is warm. Ask the model if it did a good job guessing what the user said X seconds ago while the context is cached. Use it as training data. IDK Iâm not a scientist.

FIN

Oh god Iâve spent so long on this blog post. Please upvote on your favorite link aggregator of choice.

Iâm about to YOLO into a startup, so hit me up if youâre interested in acquiring a slice of Kixel, Corp. You get a discount while Iâm spiritually unemployed and easy to impress.

Also hit me up if youâre tired of being well paid and want to YOLO into a job. Thereâs already a second nerd starting next month.

entry.title: Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says
entry.content:
The energy needed to cool the world’s buildings is overtaking the energy needed to heat them for the first time in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on November 19, 2026. The IEA, an intergovernmental agency that advises governments on energy, made the finding in the World Energy Outlook 2026, its main annual report. “Already today, for the first time in energy history, demand for cooling in buildings is overtaking that for heating,” the report’s executive summary says.

Two forces drive the change: rising incomes and rising temperatures. In emerging and developing economies outside China, 85% of households are exposed to high temperatures for at least part of the year. Fewer than one in five households there own an air conditioner.

In the IEA’s main scenario, a projection built on the policies governments have announced, the electricity used for cooling worldwide grows by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours; the kilowatt-hour is the unit on a household power bill. That increase is roughly India’s total electricity demand today.

A first in energy history

The IEA’s press release calls the shift “a striking milestone”: “energy needs to keep buildings cool are now overtaking energy needs for heating them for the first time in history.”

Most of this year’s report deals with the oil and gas shock caused by disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The cooling finding comes from another part of the report, on what people use energy for: getting around, heating, cooling and computing. The IEA calls these uses energy services.

Of these services, cooling adds the most new demand. Cooling demand in buildings has risen 55% since 2015, the IEA says in its full report. In every scenario the agency models, cooling accounts for more than 40% of the growth in energy services worldwide through 2035.

That growth comes mostly from hot countries that are getting richer. It also comes from places where cooling used to be a minor need. The report names Europe, where heat waves and warmer summers are turning cooling into a new source of demand. It cites record heat waves there and strong air conditioner sales in European countries that historically needed little cooling.

The IEA notes that August 2026 was the hottest month on record worldwide. Since mid-June, the sea surface has also set a heat record for the date every day.

Who has air conditioning, and who doesn’t

Air conditioner ownership varies widely. In Australia, Japan and the United States, around 90% of households own at least one unit, according to the report. In India and Indonesia, fewer than one in five do, despite high cooling needs. Worldwide, around 80% of the population lives in places that need cooling for at least part of the year, and around 40% of households own an air conditioner.

In emerging and developing economies outside China, the IEA projects that ownership will rise from under 20% of households today to 32% by 2035 and 45% by 2050. The projection is the same in all its scenarios. The IEA also models a current policies scenario, which counts only the policies already in place. In that scenario, more than 85% of the growth in the world’s stock of home air conditioners over the next decade happens in emerging and developing economies, China included.

By the middle of the century, the IEA projects, the world’s buildings will have more cooled floor space than heated floor space.

More electricity for cooling, and a heat-wave what-if

In the main scenario, which the IEA calls the Stated Policies Scenario, the electricity used to cool buildings rises by 1,700 TWh by 2035. It goes from about 3,000 TWh a year today to 4,700 TWh a year.

The report also models a “heatwave case,” a what-if kept apart from the main scenario. In it, heat waves become stronger, more frequent and longer, so more households buy air conditioners and use them more. In that case, cooling demand grows by 700 TWh more than in the main scenario by 2035. That is 40% more growth.

Cooling also weighs more on power grids than its share of total use suggests. Air conditioners run hardest at the same time, on the hottest days. That drives up peak demand, the highest demand a grid must meet during the year. In the main scenario, cooling makes up only 12% of the world’s electricity demand in 2035, but 30% of peak demand.

Peak demand is measured in gigawatts (GW), which count power at a single moment, while terawatt-hours count energy used over a period. Added up across the world’s power systems, it is 4,700 GW today. It grows by about 40% by 2035, in both the main scenario and the current policies scenario. Under current policies, the cooling part of the peak alone grows by 720 GW, more than India’s entire power generating capacity today.

In the main scenario, cooling and appliances together add 2,900 TWh of electricity demand by 2035. That is more electricity than the whole European Union uses today. Almost 90% of that growth happens in emerging and developing economies.

Heating still consumes more energy

Measured by the fuel and electricity consumed, heating is still well ahead. “Globally, there is less cooling than heating demand, but more electric cooling than electric heating demand,” the report says in its section on buildings. Space heating, which keeps rooms warm, uses about a third of all the energy consumed in buildings, more than any other use.

The milestone uses a different yardstick. In the report’s framing, the comparison is about energy services, meaning the comfort delivered. The sentence about cooling overtaking heating sits in the report’s section on demand for energy services. The IEA measures those services as “useful energy”: the energy that does the job people want, such as “the heat produced by a heater.”

By our reading, the two findings fit together because of how the equipment works. A boiler burns fuel and loses part of its energy in the process. An air conditioner, like a heat pump, moves heat from one place to another, so it delivers more cooling than the electricity it consumes.

The report counts air conditioners and heat pumps as devices whose output exceeds the energy they take in. That, by our reading, is why cooling can overtake heating in the service delivered while heating still consumes more energy.

The executive summary puts no number on the crossing itself. It is a result of the IEA’s modeling, and the agency describes the crossing as under way (“is overtaking”). None of the report’s scenarios is a forecast, as the IEA’s executive director, Fatih Birol, said in the press release.

In advanced economies, heating remains the largest energy service. It declines only slowly, as better insulation and warmer average temperatures offset the effect of rising incomes.

What it means

Air conditioners are spreading in the countries where most of the world’s people live. In the IEA’s projections, the share of households that own one in emerging and developing economies outside China more than doubles by 2050. Those households gain comfort, and power grids must carry a bigger load in the hottest hours of the year. Electric trucks, cars and heat pumps add to the load on those grids as well.

Electricity already supplied 23% of the energy consumed worldwide in 2025, and the IEA sees that share closing in on 30% by 2035. The agency says at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines are needed over the next ten years. On the supply side, solar covered more of the growth in world energy demand in 2025 than any other source, a first for a renewable source, according to the IEA. In the European Union, solar became the biggest source of electricity over the summer.

Efficiency rules also shape demand. Minimum efficiency standards are the legal floor on how efficient an appliance must be to go on sale. For household appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines, lighting and televisions, the IEA calculates that bringing every country up to the strictest standards in force today would save 800 TWh of electricity by 2035, almost half of it from refrigerators alone. For cooling, the current policies scenario keeps those standards at today’s levels, and cooling demand reaches 4,900 TWh by 2035, compared with 4,700 TWh in the main scenario.

Sources As an unprecedented shock reshapes the energy world, its duration will determine the scale of the change, International Energy Agency (press release), November 19, 2026 World Energy Outlook 2026: Executive summary, International Energy Agency, November 19, 2026 World Energy Outlook 2026 (full report, PDF), International Energy Agency, November 19, 2026

entry.title: How to Make the Ink Used to Write Hamlet and the Declaration of Independence
entry.content:
How to Make the Ink Used to Write Hamlet, the Declaration of Independence, and Beethoven’s Fifth Simon Garfield on the History of Henry Stephens’ Iconic “Indelible Writing Fluid,”

This is how to make the ink that wrote Magna Carta, Hamlet, Samuel Pepys’s Diary, Robinson Crusoe, Gulliver’s Travels, Candide, the Declaration of Independence, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Beethoven’s Fifth, Les Misérables, and everything in between. The recipe comes from the UK National Archives, written circa 1483:

To make hynke. Take gall & coporos & or vitrial quartryn & gumme of eueryche a quartryn oþer helf quartryn & a halfe quartryn of gall more & breke þe gall a ij oþer a iij & put ham togedere eueryche one in a pot & stere hyt ofte & wyƷt wythinne ij wykys after Ʒe mow wryte þer wyþ. & yf Ʒe have a quartryn of eueryche take a quarte of watyr yf halfe a quartryn of eueryche þan take half a quartre of watyr.

If that isn’t entirely clear, there are other ways. First, sit under an oak tree. Second, look for the oak galls, also known as oak apples, the hazelnut-size balls that grow when a gall wasp lays an egg within the underside of a leaf and the tree secretes tannic and gallic acids. Remove two ounces of galls, and once dried, grind them with mortar and pestle. Add a pint of water and leave for a day or two (in medieval manuals, wine and vinegar are frequent alternatives to water, being less likely to make you sick). Then strain through fine linen or gauze, and add an ounce of ferrous sulphate (the “coporos” mentioned in 1483). Now add three flakes of the fixative gum arabic (a golden-colored sap collected from acacia trees) which will also increase gloss and flow, and leave in a cool place—a windowsill is ideal—for a fortnight, stirring daily. Your rich purplish-black ink is now ready to use. (When applied, the drying of the ink can be speeded up by dusting your writing paper with a fine powder known as pounce, made from pumice stone or salt, or sometimes grated dried cuttlefish bone. A letter would then be regarded as “done and dusted.”)

This “iron gall” ink was more popular than the earlier carbon inks produced from soot and animal glue, or the smoke of pines mixed with oil, not least because it was less fugitive. But its permanence was overrated, as those examining century-old documents have discovered. Not only did the rich dark ink turn to lighter brown over time, but the ink could be highly corrosive, particularly on parchment, and especially if a manuscript was exposed to extreme temperatures. So you are advised to use gloves while working with it, and maybe even a thin mask over your mouth and nose if you’re sensitive to volatile substances, and obviously don’t let it go anywhere near your eyes. And for God’s sake use it only with a quill or dip pen, and never a fountain pen, unless you want the metal or resin barrel to corrode and clog the feeder. Apart from that, enjoy your writing.

The selling point was permanence, an ink that began as a clear blue turning to an intense black when dry.

The sudden success of the Birmingham steel-nib trade coincided—although it wasn’t coincidence at all—with the birth of England’s leading ink company. The bottles on display at the Pen Museum carry many familiar names—Pelikan, Sheaffer, Parker—but the most prominent in the nineteenth and early twentieth century is today largely forgotten, the London family firm of Stephens, a generational story that begins in late 1815 with a trainee doctor sharing digs with John Keats.

Henry Stephens was born in Holborn in 1796, and grew up near St. Albans, where his parents ran a busy coaching inn. His medical training at Guy’s and St. Thomas’s hospitals in Southwark necessitated cheap lodgings nearby, and for about a year he shared his rooms with the twenty-year-old fellow student and yet-unpublished poet, a friendship that endured beyond their training. According to Stephens’s daughter Martha Walsh, her father also wrote verse himself, and was instrumental in one of John Keats’s most famous works.

My mother told me [that] during their evening walks [they] quoted verses to each other. They were not satisfied with a line in the Endymion, Keats’ poem—“A thing of beauty is a constant joy.” Each thought, and almost together burst out “a joy for ever,” and so it was written, with mutual approval.

Highly regarded as a family doctor, Stephens’s medical reputation rests largely on his advances in hernia surgery; a treatise published in 1829, when he was thirty-three (and Keats had been dead already four years), remained the widely accepted method of correction for decades. But Stephens also had a sideline. Dissatisfied with the consistency and fugitive nature of ink for steel dip pens, he established a makeshift laboratory near his home to produce “an indelible writing fluid,” and his precise scientific training led to a formula that might be scaled up for mass production. With industrial chemistry in its infancy, his endeavours were revolutionary. The Stephens Ink Co. was registered in Southwark in 1832, with its first patent granted five years later.

By the time of the 1851 Great Exhibition in Hyde Park, the ink fluid had been joined by Stephens’s wood stains, with both winning royal approval from Prince Albert. The selling point was permanence, an ink that began as a clear blue turning to an intense black when dry. “It is smooth and pleasant to write with,” an early label claimed, “and preserves its fluidity in a remarkable manner under exposure.” Soon, all government and other official documents, including great amounts of banking and legal agreements, would only be considered final if they had been signed with Stephens Blue-Black.

It also had an excellent logo, or brand mark: a large ink blot created in 1891 when its advertising manager dropped a large ink-soaked sponge on a papered floor and drew round its splashy results.

The earliest recipes for what Stephens called his “carbonaceous black writing fluid” were closely guarded, and they remain a mystery. His patent cited only “certain improvements in manufacturing colouring matter,” while the listing of various acids and solvents suggested the process was highly flammable. By the 1870s, Henry Beasley’s The Druggist’s General Receipt Book had worked out the key ingredients for the most common carbon-based ink: commercial soda mixed in equal parts with shellac or resin, and then oxalic or tannic acid and water. The solution was boiled and cooled, and combined in a large pestle and mortar with fine lamp-black and other colourants.

The company moved to new premises in Aldersgate Street, now the Barbican, in 1860, and opened a New York office the following year. It faced two problems: a shortage of glass bottles led to the selling of its ink in stoneware designed for beer; and a growth in competition resulted in many legal disputes. With each edition of Henry Beasley’s manual, new but similar ink recipes appeared from a longer list of rival companies: Runge’s Black Writing Fluid competed with Coathupe’s Writing Fluid, and they were both up against Puscher’s Indelible Ink and Dr. Normandy’s Blue. Stephens’s superior product continued to dominate the market until the 1920s, aided by bold advertising.

“Stephens’ Ink—Blue-Black But Unbeaten,” declared the signs in shop windows, while tall enamel mercury thermometers were placed on railway platforms showing “Freezing,” “Temperate,” or “Blood Heat,” assuring travellers that its product worked in all climates. It also had an excellent logo, or brand mark: a large ink blot created in 1891 when its advertising manager dropped a large ink-soaked sponge on a papered floor and drew round its splashy results.

After Henry Stephens’s death in 1864, the business was taken over by his son, Henry Charles Stephens, who had learned his chemistry at the Royal School of Mines and was soon so committed to the family business that everyone called him “Inky.” Inky found the business lucrative, and fully exploited the advent of the fountain pen. The purity required for this new implement was far more demanding than that for a dip pen, but a Stephens advertisement boasted it had risen to the challenge. Its lack of sediment promised to “cure a bad circulation” and ensure “it cannot clog the feed channels, cannot corrode the nib, cannot harm rubber containers or moving parts.”

The opening of a large factory in Islington was accompanied by the development of a ten-acre home and research laboratory in Finchley, where Stephens served constituents for thirteen years as a Conservative MP and longer still as a local philanthropist. His huge garden is now open to the public, and its former conservatory serves as a small, charming, and rather forlorn museum. Keats, who knew nothing but a quill and homemade iron gall, realised his lasting fame in less than a decade, yet Stephens’s ink lasted more than a century and achieved no such thing. I live nearby, and have passed the house perhaps fifty times without knowing anything about the industry that had financed it; it felt good to discover a Victorian empire not founded on slavery.

The appointment-only museum (“The Stephens Collection”) contains a vivid gathering of ink bottles, advertisements and writing materials, and a solid history of the Stephens dynasty, which effectively ended in 1967 when the firm was bought by the Royal Sovereign Pencil Company. When I stopped by in early 2025, the visitor manager Melanie Wynyard was sifting through old patents and trade contracts, and regretting the economic downturn. “We’re clinging to the rock face now,” she says.

Her goal is just to keep the place open; with government cuts to heritage funding, there is limited interest in an archive of inks and adhesives. I take a photo of the thermometers and other enamels that once stood proud on railway platforms as steam trains chuffed by. Wynyard says that people send her pictures of these from all over the world. “There’s one in Beijing in Chinese. We did have one in Syria, although I doubt it’s there any more.”
