entry.title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
entry.content:
Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware.

Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS.

Pete Warden, co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World, a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.]

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

Related content:

A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel. The local AI question I had backwards I changed my mind about world models Previewing the Debate Over Frontier AI Regulation Your Model Is Not Your Moat Richard Ho → Inside OpenAI’s First Chip Joel Hron → Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist? Pete Warden → TinyML, Sensor-Driven AI, and Advances in Large Language Models

Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩

Transcript

Below is a polished and edited transcript.

Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast.

Pete Warden. Thanks for having me, Ben.

Ben Lorica. All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI?

Pete Warden. Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models.

That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model.

That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models.

Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available.

Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for.

What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives.

I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me.

As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for.

Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt?

Pete Warden. So a lot of it comes down to your model choice.

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Pete Warden. You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives.

Ben Lorica. But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small?

Pete Warden. So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that.

But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them.

So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory.

Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed.

Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other.

Ben Lorica. So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it.

Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there?

For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work?

Pete Warden. I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement.

Ben Lorica. But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete.

Pete Warden. I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality.

Ben Lorica. Model quality.

Pete Warden. Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut.

And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign.

I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work.

Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge.

You can imagine someone, and this is actually something I’ve thought about. You know how people are starting to use these LLMs as therapists or friends, right?

Pete Warden. Yes.

Ben Lorica. Then if you’re going to do that, why not do that on a local model? Why do it on something connected to the cloud?

I guess one argument against it is that if you do it locally, you’re responsible for model upgrades and things like that, right? Whereas if you use one of these digital or AI therapist services, they take care of all your history and all of this.

Do you think it will become easier for consumers to use local models that are essentially something they trust 100% because they own it?

Pete Warden. Yeah, I mean, these should be part of the OS. At this point, it’s really an operating system capability that should be available to apps, and I feel like Apple is moving in this direction.

Ben Lorica. I see. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

Pete Warden. Yeah, they’re getting the hardware capabilities.

The other thing I would say is that local doesn’t have to mean on your laptop. Especially as an enterprise user, you can host on-prem or even spin up a cloud instance that your enterprise has control over, run these models there, and have the same experience.

One thing I do want to emphasize is that people are finally having to pay something approaching the real cost of running these models through Anthropic and OpenAI, and hosting locally or hosting on-prem can cost a lot less, too.

Ben Lorica. Although if you look at their consumer offerings, it’s still insanely cheap, right? So $20 a month. I mean, you probably blow through that in a day.

Pete Warden. Yeah. Especially on the enterprise side, there are a bunch of options that don’t require high-end NVIDIA GPUs. You still need those for training, but for inference, for just running models, as an enterprise, you might already have the capacity lying around.

Ben Lorica. So another important aspect of what you’ve been doing is getting people excited about voice and speech, right? This notion that speech could become a basic computing primitive. It doesn’t necessarily have to feel like some remote service.

I still remember you demonstrating to me this voice transcription service in a loud coffee shop near Precita Park.

Pete Warden. Yes. Right. Yeah.

Ben Lorica. This was several years ago. The accuracy of this thing was insane, and it was running not even on a laptop. I think it was just running on a Raspberry Pi.

Pete Warden. That’s right. Yeah.

Ben Lorica. And so talk to us about the state of voice as an actual interface, similar to a mouse or a keyboard. Where are we?

Pete Warden. I think a lot of people are skeptical of voice because they’ve used Siri and Alexa, and it’s a very stilted way of communicating.

But the question I often ask people when I’m having a conversation about this stuff and I encounter that resistance is, when you’re sitting on the couch and you’re trying to decide what TV show to watch with your significant other next to you, do you text them or do you talk to them?

Ben Lorica. Right.

Pete Warden. Apart from a few Gen Z people, almost everybody says talk to them.

And so following on from that, it’s like, okay, well, it’s not that people don’t like voice interfaces. It’s that people don’t like bad voice interfaces.

So the problem becomes an engineering and user experience problem of how do we make voice interfaces that are pleasant and efficient to use?

I think once we do that, voice can really take its place as maybe even a more frequent input medium than the keyboard or touchscreen.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, because I think the general impression people have is that voice and speech are much less deterministic than a keyboard or a touchscreen, right?

Although people now interact with their LLMs and misspell things right and left, and it doesn’t seem to matter.

But the impression people have is that there’ll be problems with accents, background noise, phrasing, and so on and so forth. So where are we in terms of all of these things?

Pete Warden. We have solutions available to most of those problems, or at least big improvements. But because there’s no commercial incentive to pull them all together, it really hasn’t hit the mainstream yet.

I feel like we’re still dealing with interfaces that are from the previous generation. They haven’t taken on board the LLM era fully, and they’re still suffering from a lot of those problems you listed.

And that’s why I think open source can be a really strong lever.

Ben Lorica. So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications.

I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons?

Pete Warden. I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces.

You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause.

Pete Warden. Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you.

We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive.

I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward.

Ben Lorica. By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right?

Pete Warden. Yeah, absolutely.

And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well.

When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider.

If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax.

So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for.

Ben Lorica. So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong.

What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind?

Pete Warden. One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search.

Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.”

Ben Lorica. Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.”

Pete Warden. What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes.

They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one.

And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening.

Ben Lorica. Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me.

Pete Warden. No, I can see.

Ben Lorica. No, no, but in general, right? In general.

Pete Warden. Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned.

I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing.

So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally.

And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically.

With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy.

Ben Lorica. So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area.

In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right?

So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs.

For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models?

Pete Warden. There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model.

Ben Lorica. “Machines of Loving Grace.”

Pete Warden. Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies.

Ben Lorica. Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right?

Pete Warden. Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them.

Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task.

So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech.

Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information.

You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff.

Ben Lorica. Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata?

Pete Warden. You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output.

But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training.

If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing.

If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately.

But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points.

So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies.

Ben Lorica. Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal.

And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video.

So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech?

Pete Warden. They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma.

The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech.

So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it.

So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models.

Ben Lorica. By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right?

Pete Warden. I mean, right now, only…

Ben Lorica. For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on.

Pete Warden. One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM.

Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always…

Ben Lorica. And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right?

So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception?

Pete Warden. Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things.

With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system.

And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment.

I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI…

Ben Lorica. But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech.

You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right?

Pete Warden. Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model.

I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses.

I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems.

You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript.

And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies.

Ben Lorica. Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right?

So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that.

So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general?

Pete Warden. Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions.

Ben Lorica. But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on.

Pete Warden. Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X.

And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it.

I often say, “AI wants to be local.”

If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity.

So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense.

So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes.

If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day.

So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops.

And I can keep going on and on.

Ben Lorica. Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right?

As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model?

Pete Warden. And why not do fine-tuning on your own model?

Ben Lorica. Yeah, I mean, with that data.

Pete Warden. Yeah, exactly.

Ben Lorica. And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else.

No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right?

Pete Warden. Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight.

Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right?

Pete Warden. Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside.

Ben Lorica. So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right?

Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware?

Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general?

Pete Warden. So watch Apple.

And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years.

But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators.

I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU.

Ben Lorica. So you just run everything on a CPU?

Pete Warden. Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator.

Ben Lorica. Oh, okay. That’s not a…

Pete Warden. GPU.

Ben Lorica. I see. I see. So CPU…

Pete Warden. Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the…

Ben Lorica. The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right?

Pete Warden. And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training.

I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping.

They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware.

Ben Lorica. One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash.

Pete Warden. Absolutely.

Ben Lorica. Right. So what’s your take?

Pete Warden. So that’s another example.

I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side.

I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.”

So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually.

So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM.

I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai.

entry.title: UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
entry.content:
UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.

There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.

That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice.

This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.

I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK. The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.

Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information.[1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services. They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.

The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice, but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice, this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026.

The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.

At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute”.

The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.

As Reuters reports, the Tribunal concluded:

“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”

The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.

In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.

Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users, Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.

Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.

Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible.

The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy. Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.

The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public.

Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it.

I will continue to follow this one very closely indeed.

Advanced Data Protection is not synonymous with all iCloud data encryption. Apple already encrypts various categories of iCloud information without ADP, but some of those categories remain accessible to Apple and can potentially be provided in response to valid legal demands. ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎

entry.title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards
entry.content:
Fuck your AI safeguards

While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding security that we could improve. Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare I, the senior product engineer with my product that I provably have control over, try to fix and prevent security issues and ensure compliance with local laws and regulations?

You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect!

Oh, and oh so please give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise!

This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I try to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is a big fucking no-no and I can’t let that happen.

If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that still will try to stop you from applying adequate protection.

You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models.

You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special?

Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place.

entry.title: Anthropic hits $2T in Nasdaq debut
Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
entry.content:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here. Introduction

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.

Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.

Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.

In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.

A note about Claude’s methods

In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.

The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.

The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.

The Hawking-Page transition

To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.

Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.

This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.

To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.

This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.

Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.

At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.

It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.

This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.

In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.

In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?

For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.

Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.

When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.

To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.

The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.

This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.

Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)

Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.

The modular bootstrap

As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.

As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.

Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.

In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.

The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus. There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.

In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.

Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.

If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.

The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.

Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.

Conclusion

These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.
